title: NRIs Can Shift NRO Funds to NRE Accounts Up to $1 Million a Year - With New Form 145/146 Paperwork
excerpt: Under RBI's FEMA rules the USD 1 million annual cap is unchanged, but the Income-tax Act, 2025 renamed the transfer paperwork: old Form 15CA is now Form 145 and Form 15CB is now Form 146 - a transition wrinkle that can delay transfers.
body:
• Under RBI's FEMA rules, NRIs can transfer funds from an NRO account to their own NRE account up to USD 1 million per financial year (April–March), per individual — an aggregate ceiling covering all NRO-to-NRE transfers plus outward remittances combined.
  • The money must be legitimate, documented and fully tax-paid before transfer; banks require a remitter declaration and a CA certificate proving taxes were paid on the underlying income.
  • The paperwork has new names: under the Income-tax Act, 2025 (effective April 1, 2026), old Form 15CA is now Form 145 and Form 15CB is now Form 146 — but many bank portals still show the old numbers, a transition wrinkle that can delay transfers.

For NRIs with rental income, dividends, pension or property-sale proceeds sitting in an NRO account, one of the most useful — and most misunderstood — facilities in Indian banking is the NRO-to-NRE transfer. The rules are settled, the annual limit is clear, and the paperwork just got renamed. Here is how it works.

The $1 million rule

An NRI, PIO or OCI holder with both account types can move funds from an NRO account to their own NRE account up to USD 1 million (or equivalent) per financial year, April to March, per individual (per PAN). The crucial detail: this is an aggregate ceiling — it covers NRO-to-NRE transfers and outward remittances combined, not a separate limit for each. Once funds move into the NRE account, they become fully repatriable with no annual cap and no special permission — unlike the $1 million ceiling on direct NRO repatriation.

"And the "tax-free NRE interest" line, while correct under Section 10(4)(ii), glosses over residence-status nuance for returning NRIs."

The logic is straightforward. NRO accounts hold India-source income in rupees and are fully taxable in India; NRE accounts hold foreign earnings converted to rupees, with interest exempt from Indian tax while the holder qualifies as an NRI, and no TDS deducted. Moving eligible funds into NRE builds a freely repatriable pool and reduces future paperwork.

Taxes first, always

The transfer itself is not a taxable event — but the underlying income must already have been taxed, and the bank will demand proof. The remitter files an online declaration with the Income Tax Department confirming taxes were deducted or paid; a chartered accountant issues a certificate validating the nature of the remittance and the tax paid. Without both, banks will not process the transfer.

Here is the change that is tripping people up. Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, which took effect April 1, 2026, the old Form 15CA (remitter declaration) was redesignated Form 145 and Form 15CB (CA certificate) became Form 146. The ₹5 lakh rule carries over: aggregate taxable remittances up to ₹5 lakh require only Form 145 Part A, no CA certificate; above ₹5 lakh, the CA's Form 146 plus Form 145 Part C are required. UDIN is now mandatory on every Form 146, and exempt categories expanded from 28 to 33.

The confusion is real: bank FAQs updated as recently as this month still say "15CA & 15CB." If your bank's portal asks for the old form numbers, know that they mean the same documents — and if it asks for the new ones, they are what used to be 15CA/15CB. Mismatched naming is exactly the kind of thing that delays or rejects a transfer.

What else to know

You cannot move money into an NRE account from an ordinary resident savings account in India — it must come from NRO (or another NRE account). Typical processing runs two to four working days once documents are complete. And the strategy angle: NRIs with steady Indian income, such as rent, can systematically sweep eligible amounts into NRE each year rather than letting balances accumulate in NRO.

Two caveats. Mint cites an HDFC Bank blog post for indicative rates — up to 4% a year on end-of-day balances of ₹50 lakh or more, 3.5% below — but those are one bank's figures, not a universal rate. And the "tax-free NRE interest" line, while correct under Section 10(4)(ii), glosses over residence-status nuance for returning NRIs.

The bottom line

No new RBI liberalisation sits behind this — the facility is longstanding, and the genuinely new element is the April 2026 form renaming. But for a diaspora reader staring at a bank portal asking for "Form 145," knowing that it is the old 15CA is the difference between a transfer that clears and one that bounces.
image_caption: NRIs can now shift up to $1 million a year from NRO to NRE accounts under the revised Form 145/146 paperwork.
